market_context: United States/general English; USDA composition and variation in edible avocado size
title: How much fat is in an avocado, and what type is it?

seo.title: How much fat is in avocado? 50, 100, 150 and 200 g compared
seo.meta_description: 100 g of avocado provides about 15 g of fat: ~10 g monounsaturated, ~2.1 g saturated and ~1.8 g polyunsaturated. See different portions.
seo.search_intent: Look up how much fat a specific avocado portion contains and how that fat is divided by type.

excerpt: One hundred grams of avocado provides about 14.7–15 g of fat: roughly 9.8–10 g monounsaturated, 1.8 g polyunsaturated and 2.1 g saturated. A 50 g portion provides about 7.3 g of fat, while an avocado with 200 g of edible flesh contains close to 29 g. That is why 'one avocado' is not a useful fixed serving without knowing its size.
content_html:
Saying “an avocado has 30 g of fat” may be reasonable for a large fruit and badly wrong for a small one. The stable reference is edible weight: 100 g of avocado flesh provides about 14.7–15 g of fat.

That makes avocado unusual among fruits. It contains much more fat than apples, oranges, or berries, but most of that fat is monounsaturated. To interpret the number well, separate three questions: how much fat is present, what kind of fat it is, and how much avocado you are actually eating.

Fat at different avocado portion sizes

The calculations below use roughly 14.7 g of total fat per 100 g as the reference.

Edible avocadoTotal fatMonounsaturatedPolyunsaturatedSaturatedCalories
50 g~7.3 g~4.9 g~0.9 g~1.1 g~80
100 g~14.7 g~9.8 g~1.8 g~2.1 g~160
150 g~22 g~14.7 g~2.7 g~3.2 g~240
200 g~29.3 g~19.6 g~3.6 g~4.3 g~320

Most of the fat is monounsaturated. In 100 g, roughly two-thirds of the total fat falls into that category. The table also shows why fruit size matters: doubling edible flesh from 100 to 200 g nearly doubles both fat and calories.

Why “half an avocado” is not exact either

Avocados differ greatly in size, and the pit and skin do not make up an identical percentage of every fruit. If one avocado contains 150 g of edible flesh, half is about 75 g; if another contains 250 g, half is 125 g.

The first half would provide roughly 11 g of fat; the second about 18 g. That is why apps and generic serving tables that assign one fixed number to “half an avocado” are only estimates.

If you need precision, weigh the flesh after removing skin and pit. You do not have to do this forever; a few measurements can teach you what the avocados you normally buy tend to weigh.

What the fat breakdown actually looks like

Of the roughly 14.7 g of fat in 100 g of avocado, about 9.8 g is monounsaturated, mostly oleic acid. Saturated fat is around 2.1 g and polyunsaturated fat around 1.8 g.

That profile is very different from butter or some tropical fats, where saturated fat makes up a much larger share of total fat. Nutrition guidance generally favors replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat, and avocado can fit that swap when it replaces a more saturated ingredient.

That does not make avocado fat calorie-free. Fat type and total amount are different questions.

Variety and ripeness can shift the numbers

Hass dominates many markets, but other avocado varieties can be larger and differ in water and fat content. Natural variation exists even within the same variety.

Ripeness also changes texture and water distribution, although it does not suddenly turn the fruit into a completely different food nutritionally. That makes 14.7 g per 100 g a useful reference rather than a guarantee for every individual avocado.

Fat explains much of avocado's calorie content

Avocado provides about 160 calories per 100 g, compared with roughly 52 for apple and 47 for orange. The main reason is its roughly 15 g of fat, since fat contributes about 9 calories per gram.

Avocado is still about 73% water, which keeps its energy density far below nuts and oils. Almonds exceed 570 calories per 100 g, and oil is close to 900 calories per 100 g.

That prevents two opposite mistakes: avocado is not a very low-calorie fruit, but eating 100 g of avocado is also not nutritionally equivalent to eating 100 g of oil.

Fiber and food structure matter too

Along with fat, 100 g of avocado provides roughly 6–7 g of fiber, water, potassium, and other micronutrients. Its fat sits inside a plant food matrix that requires chewing and takes up volume.

That means 15 g of fat from avocado does not behave exactly like 15 g of oil poured onto a meal from a food-form perspective. The macronutrient comparison is still valid, but the whole food has additional characteristics that affect texture, volume, and fullness.

How to calculate your own portion

If you weigh 120 g of edible avocado, multiply 14.7 by 1.2 to get about 17.6 g of total fat. For a quick estimate, every 10 g of avocado supplies roughly 1.5 g of fat.

The same approach works for calories: every 10 g is roughly 16 calories. A toast topped with 60 g of avocado would contain about 9 g of fat and 96 calories from the avocado before counting bread, oil, egg, or other toppings.

The short answer

Count about 15 g of fat per 100 g of avocado, with roughly 10 g coming from monounsaturated fat. To know how much fat is in “an avocado,” you need at least an approximate edible weight.

The number is a tool for understanding portions, not a reason to treat avocado as a food that must be avoided. It simply makes comparisons with other fat sources more accurate.

faq.question: How much fat is in half an avocado?
faq.answer: It depends on size. A 75 g edible portion contains about 11 g of fat; a 100 g portion contains about 15 g.

faq.question: How much fat is in a whole avocado?
faq.answer: If it has 150 g of edible flesh, about 22 g; at 200 g, close to 29 g. Fruit size changes the answer substantially.

faq.question: How much of avocado fat is saturated?
faq.answer: About 2.1 g per 100 g, compared with roughly 9.8 g of monounsaturated fat.
